edmontosaurus:research:1.title: 2026 in archosaur paleontology (research: General non-avian dinosaur research)

facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus includes synonyms such as Anatosaurus, Anatotitan, Claosaurus annectens, and possibly Ugrunaaluk.
facts.quote: synonyms: *AnatosaurusLull & Wright, 1942 AnatotitanChapman & Brett-Surman, 1990 Claosaurus annectens Marsh, 1892 Ugrunaaluk?Mori et al., 2015

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus fossils date from the Late Cretaceous, spanning the Campanian to the end of the Maastrichtian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian to end Maastrichtian),

facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
facts.quote: authority: Lambe, 1917

facts.statement: Fossils of Edmontosaurus regalis are found in western North America from rocks dating to 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fossils of E. regalis have been found in rocks of western North America that date from the late Campanian age of the Cretaceous period 73 million years ago

facts.statement: Fossils of Edmontosaurus annectens are found in western North America from rocks dated to 65.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: while those of E. annectens were found in the same geographic region from rocks dated to the end of the Maastrichtian age, 65.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens reached lengths of up to 12 meters and an average weight of 5.6 metric tons.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus included two of the largest hadrosaurid species, with E. annectens measuring up to 12 m in length and weighing around 5.6 MT in average asymptotic body mass.

facts.statement: Exceptionally large specimens of Edmontosaurus annectens measured approximately 15 meters in length and weighed around 15.9 metric tons.
facts.quote: The exceptionally large specimens of E. annectens measured around 15 m long and weighed around 15.9 MT.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is a saurolophine hadrosaurid characterized by smaller, solid crests or fleshy combs rather than large hollow ones.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus is classified as a genus of saurolophine (or hadrosaurine) hadrosaurid, a member of the group of hadrosaurids that lacked large, hollow crests and instead had smaller, solid crests or fleshy combs.

facts.statement: The first fossils of Edmontosaurus were discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of southern Alberta.
facts.quote: The first fossils named Edmontosaurus were discovered in southern Alberta (named after Edmonton, the capital city), in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation (formerly called the lower Edmonton Formation).

facts.statement: The type species Edmontosaurus regalis was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
facts.quote: The type species, E. regalis, was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917, although several other species that are now classified in Edmontosaurus were named earlier.

facts.statement: The species Edmontosaurus annectens was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892.
facts.quote: The best known of these is E. annectens, named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens was originally classified as Claosaurus, later as Trachodon, and then as Anatosaurus annectens.
facts.quote: This species was originally known as a species of Claosaurus, known for many years as a species of Trachodon, and later known as Anatosaurus annectens.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was distributed across western North America, from Colorado to the northern slopes of Alaska.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus was widely distributed across western North America, ranging from Colorado to the northern slopes of Alaska.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a herbivore capable of moving on both two and four legs.
facts.quote: It was a herbivore that could move on both two legs and four.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence reveals details about Edmontosaurus, including its brain, feeding methods, and injuries such as tyrannosaur attacks.
facts.quote: The wealth of fossils has allowed researchers to study its paleobiology in detail, including its brain, how it may have fed, and its injuries and pathologies, such as evidence for tyrannosaur attacks on a few specimens.

facts.statement: In 2025, researchers detected ancient hydroxyproline in an Edmontosaurus fossil, confirming the presence of original dinosaur organic material and refuting contamination hypotheses.
facts.quote: In an Edmontosaurus fossil, Tuinstra et al. (2025) made the first clear detection of actual original dinosaur organic material, showing the presence of ancient hydroxyproline (a building block of collagen) in the fossil, and refuting the hypothesis that organic matter present in fossils must be due to contamination.

facts.statement: The specimens for Claosaurus annectens were collected in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher from the Lance Formation of Wyoming.
facts.quote: Both were collected in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher from the late Maastrichtian-age Upper Cretaceous Lance Formation of Niobrara County (then part of Converse County), Wyoming.

facts.statement: The mummified specimen AMNH 5060 was discovered in 1908 by Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his sons near Lusk, Wyoming.
facts.quote: The first, the "mummified" specimen AMNH 5060, was discovered in 1908 by Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his sons in Lance Formation rocks near Lusk, Wyoming.

facts.statement: The Sternbergs sold specimen SM 4036, which included skin impressions, to the Senckenberg Museum in Germany.
facts.quote: They sold the specimen, SM 4036, to the Senckenberg Museum in Germany.

facts.statement: The genus Edmontosaurus was named in 1917 by Lawrence Lambe based on partial skeletons discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of southern Alberta.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus itself was coined in 1917 by Lawrence Lambe for two partial skeletons found in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation (formerly the lower Edmonton Formation) along the Red Deer River of southern Alberta.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Edmontosaurus was discovered in 1912 by Levi Sternberg.
facts.quote: It was discovered in 1912 by Levi Sternberg.

facts.statement: Charles Mortram Sternberg named the species Thespesius saskatchewanensis in 1926 based on a skull and partial skeleton found on the Wood Mountain plateau of southern Saskatchewan.
facts.quote: In 1926, Charles Mortram Sternberg named Thespesius saskatchewanensis for NMC 8509, which is a skull and partial skeleton from the Wood Mountain plateau of southern Saskatchewan.

facts.statement: The rocks containing Edmontosaurus fossils are older than the rocks containing Claosaurus annectens fossils.
facts.quote: These rocks are older than the rocks in which Claosaurus annectens was found.

facts.statement: In 1942, Lull and Wright created the genus Anatosaurus to classify several hadrosaurid species that did not fit into existing genera.
facts.quote: In 1942, Lull and Wright attempted to resolve the complicated taxonomy of crestless hadrosaurids by naming a new genus, Anatosaurus, to take in several species that did not fit well under their previous genera.

facts.statement: The genus Anatosaurus is now considered a junior synonym of Edmontosaurus after its type species was reassigned.
facts.quote: Because the type species of Anatosaurus (A. annectens) was sunk into Edmontosaurus, the name Anatosaurus is abandoned as a junior synonym of Edmontosaurus.

facts.statement: The correct taxonomic classification of the specimens formerly known as Anatosaurus copei remains a subject of debate.
facts.quote: The debate about the proper taxonomy of the A. copei specimens continues to the present day.

facts.statement: A 2011 study by Nicolás Campione and David Evans used morphometric analysis to compare specimens assigned to Edmontosaurus.
facts.quote: In a 2011 study by Nicolás Campione and David Evans, the authors conducted the first ever morphometric analysis to compare the various specimens assigned to Edmontosaurus.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is currently recognized as having two valid species: E. regalis and E. annectens.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus is currently regarded as having two valid species: the type species E. regalis and E. annectens.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus regalis is known exclusively from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, dating to the late Campanian age of the late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: E. regalis is known only from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, dating from the late Campanian age of the late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens is found in the Frenchman Formation of Saskatchewan, the Hell Creek Formation of Montana, the Lance Formation of South Dakota and Wyoming, and the Ferris Formation of Wyoming.
facts.quote: E. annectens is known from the Frenchman Formation of Saskatchewan, the Hell Creek Formation of Montana, the Lance Formation of South Dakota and Wyoming and the Ferris Formation of Wyoming.

facts.statement: Specimens from the Prince Creek Formation of Alaska formerly assigned to Edmontosaurus were classified as the separate species Ugrunaaluk kuukpikensis in 2015.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurine specimens from the Prince Creek Formation of Alaska formerly assigned to Edmontosaurus sp. were given their own genus and species name, Ugrunaaluk kuukpikensis, in 2015.

facts.statement: A 2017 study questioned the validity of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus, suggesting it is indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus specimens.
facts.quote: However, the identification of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus was questioned by a 2017 study from Hai Xing and colleagues, who regarded it as a nomen dubium that was indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2020, researchers agreed that Prince Creek remains belong to Edmontosaurus, but the specific species remains unclear due to the juvenile nature of the specimens.
facts.quote: In 2020, Ryuji Takasaki and colleagues agreed that the Prince Creek remains should be classified as Edmontosaurus, though species designation is unclear because the specimens are juveniles.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens differs from E. regalis by possessing a longer, lower, and less robust skull.
facts.quote: E. annectens differed from E. regalis by having a longer, lower, and less robust skull.

facts.statement: Anatosaurus copei and Edmontosaurus saskatchewanensis are now considered growth stages of E. annectens, representing adults and juveniles respectively.
facts.quote: Anatosaurus copei and E. saskatchewanensis are now thought to be growth stages of E. annectens, with A. copei as adults and E. saskatchewanensis as juveniles.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was one of the largest duck-billed dinosaurs to ever exist.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus was among the largest hadrosaurids ever to exist.

facts.statement: Previous estimates suggested that fully grown adults could reach 9 to 12 meters in length, with some large specimens reaching 12 to 13 meters and weighing around 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Depending on the species, previous estimates suggested that a fully grown adult could have been 9 - 12 m long and some of the larger specimens reached the range of 12 - 13 m with a body mass on the order of 4 MT.

facts.statement: Two mounted skeletons measuring 8.00 meters and 8.92 meters long are likely subadult individuals rather than fully grown adults.
facts.quote: Two mounted skeletons, USNM 2414 and YPM 2182, measure 8.00 m long and 8.92 m long, respectively. However, these are probably subadult individuals.

facts.statement: Specimens from the Museum of the Rockies suggest that Edmontosaurus annectens could have reached nearly 15 meters in length and weighed up to 15.87 metric tons, though such large individuals were likely very rare.
facts.quote: Two specimens still under study in the collection of the Museum of the Rockies - a 7.5 m tail labelled as MOR 1142 and another labelled as MOR 1609 - indicate that Edmontosaurus annectens could have grown to much larger sizes and reach nearly 15 m in length, and weighed up to 15.87 MT, but such large individuals were likely very rare.

facts.statement: The skull was roughly triangular in profile and lacked a bony cranial crest.
facts.quote: The skull was roughly triangular in profile, with no bony cranial crest.

facts.statement: The beak was toothless, with both the upper and lower beaks extended by keratinous material.
facts.quote: The beak was toothless, and both the upper and lower beaks were extended by keratinous material.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is classified as a hadrosaurid, a duck-billed dinosaur family known from the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus was a hadrosaurid (a duck-billed dinosaur), a member of a family of dinosaurs which to date are known only from the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus belongs to the Saurolophinae clade, a group of hadrosaurids that lacked hollow crests.
facts.quote: It is classified within the Saurolophinae (alternately Hadrosaurinae), a clade of hadrosaurids which lacked hollow crests.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is the namesake genus of the tribe Edmontosaurini, which includes Shantungosaurus, Kerberosaurus, and Laiyangosaurus.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus is the namesake genus of the saurolophine tribe Edmontosaurini, which also includes taxa like Shantungosaurus, Kerberosaurus and Laiyangosaurus.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a large terrestrial herbivore.
facts.quote: As a hadrosaurid, Edmontosaurus was a large terrestrial herbivore.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus had dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth that were continually replaced, with only a few in use at any time.
facts.quote: Its teeth were continually replaced and packed into dental batteries that contained hundreds of teeth, only a relative handful of which were in use at any time.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus used its broad beak to crop vegetation or strip leaves and shoots from twigs and branches in a clamshell-like manner.
facts.quote: It used its broad beak to cut loose food, perhaps by cropping, or by closing the jaws in a clamshell-like manner over twigs and branches and then stripping off the more nutritious leaves and shoots.

facts.statement: Anatomical details suggest Edmontosaurus had cheek-like structures, muscular or non-muscular, to retain food in the mouth.
facts.quote: Because the tooth rows are deeply indented from the outside of the jaws, and because of other anatomical details, it is inferred that Edmontosaurus and most other ornithischians had cheek-like structures, muscular or non-muscular.

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus fed on vegetation ranging from ground level to approximately 4 meters above.
facts.quote: The animal's feeding range would have been from ground level to around 4 m above.

facts.statement: In high latitude regions like Alaska, conifers were likely the dominant food source for Edmontosaurus, though its diet was seasonally variable.
facts.quote: In high latitude regions like Alaska, conifers would have been the dominant food source, although the diet of Edmontosaurus would have been seasonally variable.

facts.statement: There is a debate over whether plant fossils found in an Edmontosaurus specimen represent gut contents or were washed in after death.
facts.quote: Kräusel, who described the material, interpreted it as the gut contents of the animal, while Abel could not rule out that the plants had been washed into the carcass after death.

facts.statement: Reports of gastroliths in the dinosaur Claosaurus were based on a misidentification of an Edmontosaurus specimen.
facts.quote: Reports of gastroliths, or stomach stones, in the hadrosaurid Claosaurus is actually based on a probable double misidentification.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown discovered the specimen in 1900 and initially referred to it as Claosaurus because Edmontosaurus annectens was then thought to be a species of Claosaurus.
facts.quote: Barnum Brown, who discovered the specimen in 1900, referred to it as Claosaurus because E. annectens was thought to be a species of Claosaurus at the time.

facts.statement: Researchers study Edmontosaurus diet and physiology by analyzing stable isotopes of carbon and oxygen preserved in tooth enamel.
facts.quote: Enamel is typically used because the structure of the mineral that forms enamel makes it the most resistant material to chemical change in the skeleton.

facts.statement: Early 2000s research challenged the prevailing model of how Edmontosaurus processed food proposed by David B. Weishampel.
facts.quote: Work in the early 2000s has challenged the Weishampel model.

facts.statement: A 2009 study identified four classes of scratches on Edmontosaurus teeth, indicating complex jaw movements during feeding.
facts.quote: Vincent Williams and colleagues (2009) published additional work on hadrosaurid tooth microwear. They found four classes of scratches on Edmontosaurus teeth.

facts.statement: A 2012 study found motions required for the Weishampel model unlikely and favored a model where lower jaw movements produced grinding action.
facts.quote: Further research published in 2012 by Robin Cuthbertson and colleagues found the motions required for Weishampel's model to be unlikely, and favored a model in which movements of the lower jaw produced grinding action.

facts.statement: Researchers interpreted skull size correlations as strong evidence that Edmontosaurus skull shape changed dramatically during growth.
facts.quote: Campione and Evans interpreted these results as strongly suggesting that the shape of Edmontosaurus skulls changed dramatically as they grew.

facts.statement: A 2014 study proposed that E. regalis reached maturity between 10 and 15 years of age.
facts.quote: In a 2014 study, researchers proposed that E. regalis reached maturity in 10-15 years of age.

facts.statement: The brain cavity of Edmontosaurus occupied about a quarter of the skull length and held endocasts ranging from 374 ml to 450 ml.
facts.quote: The space holding it was only about a quarter of the length of the skull, and various endocasts have been measured as displacing 374 ml to 450 ml

facts.statement: A specimen with a 374 ml endocast is estimated to have had a brain volume of 268 ml.
facts.quote: For example, the brain of the specimen with the 374 millilitre endocast is estimated to have had a volume of 268 ml

facts.statement: The neural canal in the hips of Edmontosaurus was expanded, though less so than in Stegosaurus.
facts.quote: Like Stegosaurus, the neural canal was expanded in the hips, but not to the same degree

facts.statement: In 2003, researchers described evidence of various tumors, including hemangiomas and metastatic cancer, in Edmontosaurus bones.
facts.quote: In 2003, evidence of tumors, including hemangiomas, desmoplastic fibroma, metastatic cancer, and osteoblastoma, was described in Edmontosaurus bones

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus fossils show osteochondrosis, a condition characterized by surficial pits in bones where they articulate.
facts.quote: Osteochondrosis, or surficial pits in bone at places where bones articulate, is also known in Edmontosaurus

facts.statement: Osteochondrosis was found in 2.2% of 224 examined Edmontosaurus toe bones.
facts.quote: This condition, resulting from cartilage failing to be replaced by bone during growth, was found to be present in 2.2% of 224 edmontosaur toe bones

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was a facultative biped, primarily moving on four legs but capable of standing or moving on two legs.
facts.quote: Like other hadrosaurids, Edmontosaurus is thought to have been a facultative biped, meaning that it mostly moved on four legs, but could adopt a bipedal stance when needed

facts.statement: Computer modeling from 2007 suggests Edmontosaurus could run at speeds up to 45 km/h.
facts.quote: Research conducted by computer modeling in 2007 suggests that Edmontosaurus could run at high speeds, perhaps up to 45 km/h

facts.statement: Computer simulations indicated a maximum simulated speed of 17.3 m/s for a kangaroo-like hopping gait, though researchers considered this unlikely.
facts.quote: The researchers found to their surprise that the fastest gait was kangaroo-like hopping (maximum simulated speed of 17.3 m/s)

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus had slim hands with short fingers, rendering its forelimbs ineffective for swimming propulsion.
facts.quote: Hadrosaurids had slim hands with short fingers, making their forelimbs ineffective for propulsion

facts.statement: Unlike many other hadrosaurids, Edmontosaurus did not possess a bony crest.
facts.quote: Unlike many other hadrosaurids, Edmontosaurus lacked a bony crest

facts.statement: Some authors consider Edmontosaurus to have been a possibly migratory hadrosaurid.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus has been considered a possibly migratory hadrosaurid by some authors

facts.statement: A study of bone microstructure by Anusuya Chinsamy and colleagues concluded that polar Edmontosaurus overwintered, contradicting migration hypotheses.
facts.quote: In contrast to Bell and Snively, Anusuya Chinsamy and colleagues concluded from a study of bone microstructure that polar Edmontosaurus overwintered

facts.statement: The Horseshoe Canyon Formation, where Edmontosaurus regalis is found, dates from approximately 73 million years ago to between 68.0 and 67.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Deposition began approximately 73 million years ago, in the late Campanian, and ended between 68.0 and 67.6 million years ago

facts.statement: The Lance Formation, located approximately 100 km north of Fort Laramie in eastern Wyoming, is interpreted as a bayou setting.
facts.quote: The Lance Formation, as typified by exposures approximately 100 km north of Fort Laramie in eastern Wyoming, has been interpreted as a bayou setting

facts.statement: The Lance Formation preserves two Edmontosaurus "mummies".
facts.quote: The Lance Formation is the setting of two edmontosaur "mummies"

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus regalis lived in western North America between 73 and 70 million years ago during the late Campanian.
facts.quote: Se han encontrado fósiles de E. regalis en rocas del oeste de Norteamérica que datan de fines del Campaniano entre 73 a 70 millones de años

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus annectens lived in the same western North American region between 68 and 66 million years ago during the late Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: mientras que las de E. annectens se encontraron en la misma región geográfica, pero en rocas que datan de finales del Maastrichtiano, entre 68 a 66 millones de años

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs, living alongside Triceratops, Tyrannosaurus, Pachycephalosaurus, and Ankylosaurus shortly before the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus fue uno de los últimos dinosaurios no aviares, y vivió junto a dinosaurios como Triceratops, Tyrannosaurus, Pachycephalosaurus y Ankylosaurus poco antes de la extinción masiva del Cretácico-Paleógeno

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus included some of the largest hadrosaurid species, reaching lengths of up to 12 meters and weighing around 4 tons.
facts.quote: Edmontosaurus incluyó algunas de las especies de hadrosáuridos más grandes, midiendo hasta 12 metros de largo y pesando alrededor de 4 toneladas

facts.statement: Two specimens housed at the Royal Tyrrell Museum suggest that Edmontosaurus annectens could reach a maximum size of 15 meters in length and 10 tons in weight.
facts.quote: Existe evidencia en forma de dos especímenes fosilizados alojados en el Museo de las Rocosas para un tamaño máximo aún mayor de 15 metros y un peso de 10 toneladas para Edmontosaurus annectens

facts.statement: Several well-preserved Edmontosaurus specimens include not only bones but also extensive skin impressions and possible gut contents.
facts.quote: Se conocen varios especímenes bien conservados que incluyen no solo huesos, sino en algunos casos impresiones extensas de piel y posible contenido intestinal

facts.statement: Evidence of multiple bone beds suggests that Edmontosaurus lived in groups and may have been migratory.
facts.quote: Debido a que se sabe de varios lechos óseos, se cree que Edmontosaurus vivió en grupos y también pudo haber sido migratorio

facts.statement: The first Edmontosaurus fossils were discovered in southeastern Alberta, Canada, in the area known as the "Lower Edmonton" within the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Edmontosaurus fueron descubiertos al sureste de Alberta, Canadá, en la zona usualmente llamada "Edmonton inferior" que pertenece a la Formación Cañón Herradura

facts.statement: The type species, Edmontosaurus regalis, was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
facts.quote: La especie tipo, E. regalis, fue nombrada por Lawrence Lambe en 1917

facts.statement: The most famous species, Edmontosaurus annectens, was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892.
facts.quote: La más conocida de estas probablemente sea E. annectens, nombrada por Othniel Charles Marsh en 1892

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus is classified as a saurolophine (or hadrosaurine) hadrosaurid, a group characterized by lacking large hollow crests and instead possessing smaller solid crests or fleshy combs.
facts.quote: Se clasifica como un género de saurolofino (o hadrosaurino) hadrosáurido, un miembro del grupo de hadrosáuridos que carecía de crestas grandes y huecas, y en su lugar tenía crestas sólidas más pequeñas o peines carnosos

facts.statement: Edmontosaurus possessed a long laterally flattened tail and a large head with a wide, semispherical duck-like beak filled with small teeth used to crush its food.
facts.quote: Poseía una larga cola aplanada lateralmente y en su gran cabeza tenía un amplio pico semiesférico similar al de un pato en su boca llena de pequeños dientes con los que trituraba su alimento

facts.statement: Adult Edmontosaurus sizes varied considerably by species and individual, ranging from 9 meters with some specimens reaching 13 meters to 14 meters in length.
facts.quote: Las proporciones de los Edmontosaurus varían considerablemente según la especie e individuo, presentando tamaños en adultos que van desde los 9 metros con especímenes de 13 metros, hasta los 14 metros de largo

facts.statement: Two specimens under study at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, including a 7.6-meter tail labeled MOR 1142 and another labeled MOR 1609, suggest that E. annectens could have grown larger, possibly rivaling Shantungosaurus in size.
facts.quote: Dos especímenes aún en estudio en la colección del Museo de las Rocosas, una cola de 7,6 metros etiquetada como MOR 1142 y otra etiquetada como MOR 1609, indican que E. annectens podría haber crecido a tamaños más grandes, posiblemente rivalizando con Shantungosaurus en tamaño

facts.statement: The top of the tail of the Denver specimen was at least 2.9 meters high, a height only reachable by T. rex from the same rock formation.
facts.quote: The top of the tail was at least 2.9 m high, and the only theropod species known from the same rock formation that was tall enough to make such an attack is T. rex

facts.statement: The bite marks on the Denver specimen show signs of bone infection.
facts.quote: The damage also shows signs of bone infection

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter suggested the edmontosaur was targeted because it may have been limping from a prior healed fracture in the left hip.
facts.quote: He suggested that the edmontosaur was a target because it may have been limping from this earlier injury

facts.statement: More modern studies dispute the idea that the tail damage on the Denver specimen resulted from a tyrannosaur attack, suggesting other unrelated factors instead.
facts.quote: However, more modern studies dispute the idea of an attack but rather other factors unrelated to an attack from a tyrannosaur

facts.statement: Some of the tooth marks on the South Dakota specimen are partially healed.
facts.quote: Some of the marks are partially healed

facts.statement: Michael Triebold suggested that small theropods attacked the throat of the South Dakota specimen, which survived the initial attack but died shortly after from its injuries.
facts.quote: Michael Triebold, informally reporting on the specimen, suggested a scenario where small theropods attacked the throat of the edmontosaur; the animal survived the initial attack but succumbed to its injuries shortly thereafter

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest that all evidence for Daspletosaurus presence in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation should be attributed to Albertosaurus instead.
facts.quote: However more recent studies suggest that any and all evidence for Daspletosaurus being present in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation is referrable to Albertosaurus

facts.statement: The skull of a fully developed Edmontosaurus measures around 1 meter in length.
facts.quote: El cráneo de un ejemplar completamente desarrollado de Edmontosaurus media alrededor de 1 metro de largo.

facts.statement: The skull of E. annectens, formerly known as Anatotitan, measures 1.18 meters in length.
facts.quote: Un cráneo de E. annectens, anteriormente Anatotitan, mide 1,18 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The beak had no teeth and was covered by a horny keratinous sheath on both the upper and lower jaws.
facts.quote: El pico no poseía dientes, y tanto la parte superior y la inferior poseían un pico córneo de queratina

facts.statement: Teeth were located only in the cheeks, on the maxilla in the upper jaw and the dentary in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Los dientes solo se encuentran en las mejillas, sobre el hueso maxilar en la parte superior y en el dentario en la inferior.

facts.statement: Teeth grew in columns, with at least six teeth in a single column.
facts.quote: Estos dientes crecían en columnas, con hasta por lo menos seis dientes en una columna

facts.statement: The anterior part of the back curved toward the ground, with the neck bent upward and the rest of the back and tail held horizontally.
facts.quote: La porción anterior de la espalda se curvaba hacia el suelo, con el cuello doblado hacia arriba y el resto de la espalda y de la cola sostenidas horizontalmente.

facts.statement: Most of the back and tail were reinforced by a network of ossified tendons between the vertebral spines.
facts.quote: La mayor parte del lomo y la cola estaba reforzado por un enrejado de tendones osificados entre las espinas de las vértebras.

facts.statement: The pelvis consisted of three elements on each side: an elongated ilium above the hind leg joint, an ischium below and behind as a long thin rod, and a pubis in front that expanded into a perforated plate-like structure.
facts.quote: La pelvis se componía por tres elementos a cada lado, un alargado ilion por encima de la articulación de la pata trasera, el isquion por debajo y por detrás como una varilla larga y delgada y el pubis en el frente que se dilataba en una estructura similar a una placa y perforado.

facts.statement: Each hand had four fingers, lacking the first digit.
facts.quote: Cada mano tenía cuatro dedos, sin el primer dedo.

facts.statement: The second, third, and fourth fingers were approximately the same length and were united in life within a fleshy covering.
facts.quote: Los dedos segundo, tercero y cuarto tenían aproximadamente la misma longitud y estaban unidos en la vida dentro de una cubierta carnosa.

facts.statement: Each foot had only three toes, lacking the first and fifth digits.
facts.quote: Cada pie tenía solo tres dedos de los pies, sin dedo primero y el quinto.

facts.statement: Skin impressions are less known for E. regalis, but some well-preserved examples have been studied, including one preserving a soft tissue crest or beard on the head.
facts.quote: Las impresiones de la piel son menos conocidas para E. regalis, pero se han estudiado algunos ejemplos bien conservados, incluido uno que conserva una cresta de tejido blando o una barba en la cabeza.

facts.statement: A preserved rhamphotheca in specimen LACM 23502 indicates that the Edmontosaurus beak was more hooked and extensive than previously illustrated in scientific and public media.
facts.quote: Una rhamphotheca preservada presente en el espécimen de E. annectens LACM 23502, ubicado en el Museo de Historia Natural del Condado de Los Ángeles, indica que el pico de Edmontosaurus era más ganchudo y extenso de lo que muchas ilustraciones en medios científicos y públicos han descrito anteriormente.

facts.statement: Although Edmontosaurus was named in 1917, its oldest well-supported species, E. annectens, was named in 1892 as a species of Claosaurus.
